rows.label: Concept
rows.text: GPS places 24+ satellites in six orbital planes at ~20 200 km with 12-hour periods — orbits computed from the same gravitation as any satellite: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, $T^2 \propto r^3$. Each satellite broadcasts an atomic-clock timestamp; the receiver multiplies travel time by $c$ to get pseudoranges and **trilaterates**: three satellites fix a position, the fourth solves the receiver's clock error.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Distance = c × Δt - Orbit: v = √(GM/r); T = 2π√(r³/GM) ≈ 12 h at 20 200 km - Clock correction ≈ +38 μs/day

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **GPS ≠ geostationary:** 24+ satellites at 20 200 km, 12-hour periods, six planes — designed for whole-Earth coverage.  ·  **The fourth satellite fixes your clock,** not just your position.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "A GPS receiver computes its position by measuring the travel time of signals from at least four satellites."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Constellation*** — 24+ satellites, 20 200 km, T ≈ 12 h: any point on Earth always sees 4+.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: No verified PYQ; NEB-style practice (principle 4m, four-satellite reasoning 2m, applications 2m).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Gravity as Navigation The Global Positioning System puts 24+ satellites in precisely known orbits and asks a simple question: how long does a radio signal take to reach me? Time-of-flight gives distance; distance from four satellites pins down position. Newton's gravitation determines the orbits; relativity corrects the clocks.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 How GPS works 1. **Constellation:** at least 24 satellites in six orbital planes, ~20 200 km altitude, period ≈ 12 hours — visible from any point on Earth at any time (4+ satellites overhead). 2. **Each satellite broadcasts** its identity, exact orbital position and an atomic-clock timestamp. 3. **Receiver measures signal travel time** $t$; distance = $c \times t$ (pseudorange). 4.…

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Short (2m): Why does GPS need four satellites, not three?** — Three spheres intersect in two points and leave the receiver clock error uncorrected; the fourth measurement solves for the clock offset along with the three coordinates.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Describe the four steps: broadcast, time-of-flight, pseudorange, trilateration — then the corrections.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Time becomes distance:** because c is known, measuring time-of-flight measures position — the clock correction is gravitational physics.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Distance = c × time-of-flight; four satellites → latitude, longitude, altitude, clock error.  ·  Relativistic correction ≈ 38 μs/day; without it positions drift ~10 km/day.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: GPS satellites carry atomic clocks (cesium/rubidium) accurate to ~1 ns — timing errors of 1 μs mean 300 m of position error.
